source_text: So, independent of the tech week no-bots blocker, I think we could start to set up an improved version of the futon "forward model" that takes into account some of our techweek scanning.  We could in principle use other open source intelligence to feed into that model (although my Claude usage is low right now so I'll save any deep research tasks for another time).  What occurs to me is that customer journeys and development trajectories are closely related, i.e., if we were getting lots of people clicking on the xiao-xiang demo but had no concrete offer we'd know that there was "demand" but it wouldn't be clear for what.  In reality, I'm not sure how many people would click on the open source offering, so we probably need to think more about what *would* draw people in.  While you've phrased the questions above as "find the pain rather than pitch" the forward model could map pain points to a likely build out that would address the need.  As for leaving active inference out of the pitch, one clever idea would be to keep going with the active inference work (which itself is a locus of information about a forward model) but "close it" over operator turns as described in the futon-2026 working paper.  Assuming it is useful for *me* then I'd be able to show good work-product while keeping AIF as a semi-secret-sauce.  (Not a real secret b/c it is published by others and I myself am publicly working on the PLoP-2026 paper and have all my code on Github.)  But it's worth being clear that I have some hypotheses about what would be "missing" at XTrace & Tessl and it is that in short they don't have AIF models or anything close to it.  That matters if what we're doing is not just optimizing agent chats but optimizing overall behaviour in organisations.  (And the latter should not be hard to sell *if it is demonstrated*, though it may rightly very be hard to sell if it is not!)

reply_text:
I'm reading the existing forward-model mission and the paper's Part II, then I'll write a small demand-side extension to the model.㊥ Gist: I've added a demand side to the forward model. It maps pain points to the build-out that would address each one, and it rates each way someone could reach us by how much it says about *which* pain they have. The step that ties this to your active inference work: record whether you accepted, declined or ignored each agent proposal, using the reply marks agents started using yesterday. That is the paper's Part II loop closed over your turns. The same pairing would power the pilot, so building it once gives you a demo of both.

㊢ (what's written, `futon7/holes/M-futon-forward-model.demand-v0.edn`, commit 777490b) The file sits alongside the mission's existing backlog-and-market roadmap, which covers the supply side.
- **Segments (4):** team lead, engineering org, agent founder, and a heavy solo user like you.
- **Pains (6):**
  - dropped or repeated requests
  - token cost
  - lessons from sessions not becoming team rules (what XTrace sells)
  - production observability (crowded, so not ours)
  - uncurated memory
  - follow-through in the organisation: proposals unanswered, so nobody can tell a rejection from no response (the 108 unanswered proposals from the paper's WR-0)
- **Build-outs (5), marked by whether a demo exists:** fast mode does; the rollout audit and pattern memory partly do; the request audit and proposal recording don't.
- **Hypotheses (3):** each has a test, including yours about AIF.

The priors are my guesses, labelled as guesses. I did no deep research.

㊣ (your point about clicks) I agree, and the model shows what follows for the site. A click on the 小象 demo shows interest in reading intent, not in any particular build-out. A click on a page that names one pain and one offer does tell us which pain. So the 小象 page should lead to one short offer page per pain, not a general contact link. That turns the website into a source of evidence for the model.

㊭ (AIF as the part behind the demo) Since yesterday, agent replies carry a mark on each paragraph, so a proposal (㊭) or a request for a decision (🈸) can be found by script. 象 and 小象 already read your next turn. Pairing the two gives, for each proposal: accepted, declined, or no response. That is the three-way record `sec-operator.tex` says is missing. With it, the agents' proposal policy can learn from your answers, which the AIF loop needs. You would get something useful straight away: a weekly count of what you accept and ignore, by kind of proposal. It is also what you could show people without explaining active inference.

㊟ (your hypothesis about XTrace and Tessl) I recorded it as hypothesis `:h/aif-gap`. Its test is one question you can ask at Tech Week: "Does the tool change what agents propose, based on what you accepted or declined?" I also wrote the condition you stated: it sells only once shown on your own record, with a before and after.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I build proposal recording v0 over your turns since 30 September? It's a script plus one report, using marks and readings we already have.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(your point on the upsell) I agree the paid work would be the memory system, not 象 alone. I'd also leave active inference out of the pitch. A live demo of AIF loops improving your stack is the hard thing to show, and you don't need it to make the case. What is distinctive and easy to show is smaller:
- **Patterns carry outcomes:** your patterns record how they turned out when they were used. This is page 6 of the site plan, memory that has been evaluated.
- **Turns are linked:** a turn connects to the patterns and missions it touched, so "I was talking about such-and-such" finds the right material.
- **Contrast with XTrace:** XTrace's offer, sessions turned into rules, is the generic version of this. Hearing what its users find missing is the most direct test of whether your difference is worth paying for.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(different isn't necessarily valuable) I can't settle that from here. Conversations at Tech Week can, so I wrote the questions to find out where the pain is rather than to pitch:
1. How do you know an agent did what you asked?
2. Who reads agent transcripts on your team?
3. Would you let a tool run over your rollouts on your own machine?
4. What does your agents' memory hold now, and who curates it?
5. What was missing from XTrace, Tessl or similar tools you've tried?
